title: Act Fast (Like Gemini!)
caption: Gemini South and Vera C. Rubin Observatory at night, Cerro Pachón
celestial: Landscape photograph; the source does not name the site
credit: International Gemini Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/P. Horálek (Institute of Physics in Opava)

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Gemini South, which makes up half of the International Gemini Observatory, stands on Cerro Pachón in this night photograph. Behind it rises the NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which has just begun operating.

The photograph's theme is speed. A meteor may be visible for only a few seconds, and many astronomical objects change quickly. Studying these fleeting changes is called time-domain astronomy, and Gemini is often one of the observatories that follows up on fast-changing events such as supernovae, asteroids, variable stars, active galactic nuclei and meteors. In 2025, Gemini South follow-up helped astronomers characterise the nearest supernova known to be tied to a fast X-ray transient, as well as the near-Earth asteroid 2024 YR4.

Rubin works hand in hand with this kind of follow-up. As a survey telescope, it will sweep the southern sky and pick up as many as 10 million changes each night, with every one triggering an alert to astronomers within minutes.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken with a camera in visible light on Cerro Pachón. The camera settings and processing are not published.
understand.eye: A long camera exposure gathers much more light than the eye, so the night sky looks brighter and richer in stars than it would to someone standing there.
